deep.reconstruction:
PART A (end of the Pothenot/Snellius resection problem from the previous page). Notation as on p.280: the unknown station is (0); 1,2,3 are known objects; (01),(02) are the observed azimuths from 0 to 1 and 2; (12) denotes either the distance or the direction (azimuth) from 1 to 2, depending on context; 1* is a distance.

New construction. Instead of 0 itself, Gauss constructs the point * on the ray 1→0 with 1* = 1/(10). In modern terms * is the image of 0 under inversion in the unit circle centred at 1.

Why this helps (my explanation). The locus of 0 seeing 1 and 2 under the angle (02)−(01) is a circle through 1. Inversion with centre 1 sends that circle to a straight line. So * is the intersection of straight lines, one line for each object other than 1. This is Gauss's 'eine weniger als von (0) aus Objecte geschnitten sind'.

The line coming from object 2 passes through the inverse 2' of point 2. This point has polar coordinates (distance 1/(12), direction (12)) about 1.

Its angle (my justification). Inversion makes triangle 1,0,2 similar (with reversed orientation) to triangle 1,2',*. Hence the angle at 2' between 2'→1 and 2'→* equals the angle at 0 between 0→1 and 0→2, namely (02)−(01). So the line makes the angle (02)−(01) with (12), i.e. it has azimuth (21)−[(02)−(01)]. The sign of the rotation depends on orientation conventions.

Refinement. Using the power (12)·(13) instead of 1 in the numerators (inversion radius² = (12)(13)) puts 2' at distance (13) and 3' at distance (12). The construction then uses only given lengths: 'am elegantesten'.

PART B. Solution of the trinomial equation F t^f = G t^g + H t^h with Gauss's addition/subtraction-logarithm table. Write 𝔄 = F t^f, 𝔅 = G t^g, ℭ = H t^h, so 𝔄 = 𝔅 + ℭ.

Version I.
- Put 𝔄 = 𝔅b = ℭc and 𝔅 = aℭ. Then (implicit, mine) b = 1 + 1/a, c = 1 + a, and c = ab. These are exactly the quantities the Gaussian table gives from log a.
- From the definitions: t^(g−h) = aH/G, t^(f−g) = bG/F, t^(f−h) = cH/F.
- Eliminating t pairwise gives b^(f−h) c^(g−f) = a^(g−f) b^(g−h) = a^(h−f) c^(g−h) = F^(g−h) G^(h−f) H^(f−g).
- Because c = ab, these combine into a^(λ−f) b^(λ−h) c^(g−λ) = (same right side) for arbitrary λ.
- Procedure: in logarithms this is one equation in log a, with log b and log c read from the table. Solve it by trial; then t follows from any of the three power relations.

Version II ('noch zierlicher').
- Put 𝔄 = 𝔅c = ℭb and 𝔅a = ℭ. Now a = ℭ/𝔅, c = 1 + a, b = 1 + 1/a, and again c = ab.
- Then t^(h−g) = aG/H, t^(f−h) = bH/F, t^(f−g) = cG/F.
- The elimination gives a^(f−λ) b^(g−λ) c^(λ−h) = F^(g−h) G^(h−f) H^(f−g), λ arbitrary. This is equivalent to a^(f−h) b^(g−h) = F^(g−h) G^(h−f) H^(f−g).

The next page continues with the double-root condition and series/trigonometric treatment of the same trinomial.
errors: No mathematical errors found. All three power relations in both versions and all elimination identities check out.
The λ-forms are valid only by virtue of the unstated relation c = ab, which follows from b = 1+1/a, c = 1+a in I and from b = c/a in II.

The azimuth (21)−[(02)−(01)] fixes a rotation sense that depends on the orientation of the configuration. Inversion reverses orientation, so in mirrored configurations the sign would flip. This is unstated rather than an error.

results.what: Solving the Pothenot (Snellius) resection problem by inverting the unknown station about one known point: 1* = 1/(10), radius² optionally (12)(13). This turns the locus circles into straight lines whose intersection gives the image point.
results.modern_name: Inversion in a circle (transformation by reciprocal radii) applied to the resection/Snellius–Pothenot problem
results.usually_credited_to: Inversion as a geometric transformation: Steiner (c.1824–26), Plücker, Magnus (1831), Bellavitis (1836), Thomson and Liouville (1845–47). Resection problem: Snellius (1617), Pothenot (1692).

results.what: Reduction of the trinomial equation F t^f = G t^g + H t^h to a single transcendental equation in log a, solvable by Gaussian addition/subtraction logarithms, with t recovered from t^(g−h) = aH/G etc.
results.modern_name: Solution of trinomial equations using Gaussian (addition/subtraction) logarithms
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss: table of 1812; trinomial equations treated in 'Beiträge zur Theorie der algebraischen Gleichungen' (1849). Addition logarithms are also credited to Leonelli (1802).

deep.surprise_reason: The trinomial/Gaussian-logarithm material is known Gauss and largely routine. The resection construction via reciprocal radii is an explicit use of inversion to straighten circles. If this page dates from c.1810–12, that predates Steiner/Magnus/Plücker. However, point-wise reciprocal constructions were known earlier, and Gauss's Pothenot notes are partly in Werke. So this is a notable but not major priority detail.

checkable.sympy: a,G,H,F,f,g,h=symbols('a G H F f g h',positive=True); b=1+1/a; c=1+a; simplify(c-a*b)==0
checkable.asserts: In version I, c = ab, given b = 1+1/a and c = 1+a.
a^(g−f) b^(g−h) = F^(g−h) G^(h−f) H^(f−g) in version I, with a = 𝔅/ℭ, b = 𝔄/𝔅.
b^(f−h) c^(g−f) = F^(g−h) G^(h−f) H^(f−g) in version I.
a^(h−f) c^(g−h) = F^(g−h) G^(h−f) H^(f−g) in version I.
Version II identity a^(f−λ) b^(g−λ) c^(λ−h) = F^(g−h) G^(h−f) H^(f−g) for arbitrary λ, with a = ℭ/𝔅, b = 𝔄/ℭ, c = 𝔄/𝔅.
Unit inversion about point 1 (the origin): |0'2'| = |02|/(|10||12|). This underlies the similarity of triangles 1,0,2 and 1,2',*.
Numerical check: the angle at 2' in triangle (1,2',*) equals the angle at 0 between the directions to 1 and 2, i.e. (02)−(01).

transcription_corrections: In version II the last power relation t^(f−g) = cG/F has an overwritten/struck letter in the denominator; the intended reading is F, which agrees with the mathematics.
Margin note 'Sch.' (or similar) at the right of the 'Am elegantesten…' line is omitted by the transcription; it is likely a cross-reference mark.
The parenthetical reads 'nemlich Distanz 1/(12), Richtg (12)' as an interlinear insertion; the transcription is correct in substance.
